\begin{abstract}
Mathematical arguments can be represented by directed dependency networks whose vertices are statements and whose edges point from premises to statements using them. When circular justification is excluded, these networks are directed acyclic graphs. We isolate the consequences of acyclicity from empirical claims about theorem reuse. For a finite acyclic relation, the strict ancestors of a vertex are all vertices reaching it by a nonempty directed path, and its canonical rank is the number of those ancestors. We prove that rank strictly increases along reachability. We then establish a width--depth theorem: if a rank map into $L$ ordered levels strictly increases along reachability and the network has more than $L$ vertices, two distinct vertices on one level are mutually incomparable. Finally, for every $n\geq3$ we construct an acyclic network that remains weakly connected after deletion of any single vertex. These results show that hierarchy and a pigeonhole-based width principle follow from finite acyclicity, whereas power-law degree distributions, universal hub rankings, and single-hub fragility do not.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
A proof rarely depends on only one earlier statement. Definitions, lemmas, and theorems form a many-to-many system of support naturally represented as a directed graph. A vertex denotes a statement, and an edge points from a premise to a statement that directly uses it. A directed path records indirect dependence.

This model prompts two kinds of question. Structural questions ask what must hold in every finite acyclic dependency network. Empirical questions ask what patterns occur in a particular corpus under a particular extraction rule. Acyclicity is structural. A proposed power law for reuse, a list of historically dominant hubs, or a claim about damage caused by deleting a theorem is empirical. These categories must not be conflated: directed acyclic graphs include chains, trees, disconnected layered graphs, and dense total orders, with radically different degrees and robustness.

We prove three results. First, every finite acyclic network has an intrinsic topological rank given by the number of strict ancestors. Second, if a strictly increasing rank uses only $L$ levels and there are more than $L$ vertices, two vertices are forced to be incomparable. Third, for every $n\geq3$ there is an acyclic network on $n$ vertices that remains weakly connected after deletion of any vertex. Edges are oriented from prerequisite to dependent statement, and connectivity after deletion is weak connectivity, so orientation is ignored during traversal.

\section{Definitions}
Let $V$ be a finite set and $R\subseteq V\times V$ a directed relation. Write $R(u,v)$ when $v$ directly depends on $u$.

\begin{definition}[Reachability and acyclicity]
A nonempty directed path from $u$ to $v$ is a sequence $u=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m=v$, where $m\geq1$ and $R(v_{i-1},v_i)$ for each $i$. Write $u\leadsto v$ when such a path exists. The relation $R$ is \emph{acyclic} when no $v\in V$ satisfies $v\leadsto v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Strict ancestors and canonical rank]
The strict ancestor set and canonical ancestor rank of $v$ are
\[
 A(v)=\{u\in V:u\leadsto v\},\qquad \rho(v)=|A(v)|.
\]
The rank counts all distinct upstream vertices, rather than only the length of a longest chain.
\end{definition}

Two vertices are \emph{mutually incomparable} if neither reaches the other. An $L$-level strict rank map is a function
\[
 r:V\longrightarrow\{0,1,\ldots,L-1\}
\]
such that $a\leadsto b$ implies $r(a)<r(b)$.

\begin{definition}[Weak connectivity after deletion]
Fix $d\in V$. An avoiding weak walk from $a$ to $b$ is a sequence $a=w_0,\ldots,w_t=b$ in which every $w_i\neq d$ and each consecutive pair is joined by an edge in either orientation. The case $t=0$ is permitted. The network is weakly connected after deleting $d$ if every two surviving vertices admit such a walk, and is robust under single-vertex deletion if this holds for every $d$.
\end{definition}

\section{Canonical hierarchy}
\begin{lemma}[Ancestor monotonicity]
If $a\leadsto b$, then $A(a)\subseteq A(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $u\in A(a)$, concatenate a path from $u$ to $a$ with one from $a$ to $b$. This gives $u\leadsto b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Strict ancestor growth]
If $R$ is acyclic and $a\leadsto b$, then $A(a)\subsetneq A(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Monotonicity gives inclusion. Also $a\in A(b)$. Acyclicity gives $a\notin A(a)$, so the inclusion is proper.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical Topological Rank Theorem]
Let $R$ be acyclic on finite $V$. Then
\[
 a\leadsto b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho(a)<\rho(b).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Strict ancestor growth makes $A(a)$ a proper subset of the finite set $A(b)$, and proper containment strictly increases cardinality.
\end{proof}

This rank is intrinsic: no tie-breaking topological sort is required. Equal ranks need not mean equal ancestor sets, but they prevent reachability.

\begin{corollary}[Equal-rank incomparability]
If $a\neq b$ and $\rho(a)=\rho(b)$, then neither $a\leadsto b$ nor $b\leadsto a$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Either path would contradict strict rank increase.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Path-length bound]
If $v_0\to v_1\to\cdots\to v_m$ is a directed path, then
\[
0\leq\rho(v_0)<\rho(v_1)<\cdots<\rho(v_m)\leq |V|-1,
\]
and hence $m\leq |V|-1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the theorem to each edge. A vertex is not its own ancestor, so an ancestor set contains at most $|V|-1$ vertices.
\end{proof}

\section{The width--depth tradeoff}
\begin{theorem}[Width--Depth Incomparability Theorem]
Let $r:V\to\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$ strictly increase along every nonempty directed path. If $L<|V|$, then there are distinct $a,b\in V$ such that neither $a\leadsto b$ nor $b\leadsto a$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The pigeonhole principle gives distinct $a,b$ with $r(a)=r(b)$. A path in either direction would force a strict inequality between these equal ranks.
\end{proof}

Thus bounded dependency depth forces horizontal width. More vertices than legal levels cannot form one reachability chain.

\begin{proposition}[Rank-level antichain bound]
Under the preceding hypotheses, there is a set of at least
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{|V|}{L}\right\rceil
\]
pairwise mutually incomparable vertices.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A largest fiber of $r$ has at least the displayed size. Distinct vertices in one fiber cannot reach one another because reachability strictly raises rank.
\end{proof}

For canonical rank, any collision therefore certifies parallel branches of dependency. This is structural incomparability, not necessarily semantic independence: two incomparable statements may discuss the same objects or even be logically equivalent without a recorded path between them.

\section{A robust acyclic family}
For $n\geq1$, let $V_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ and define the strict total-order network $T_n$ by
\[
 R_n(i,j)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i<j.
\]
Every distinct pair has one edge, oriented from smaller to larger.

\begin{theorem}[Acyclicity of the Strict Total-Order Network]
For every $n$, the network $T_n$ is acyclic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every directed edge strictly increases the integer label. Hence every nonempty directed path from $i$ to $j$ has $i<j$, and no path can return to its start.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Robustness After Arbitrary Single-Vertex Deletion]
Let $d,a,b\in V_n$, with $a\neq d$ and $b\neq d$. There is an avoiding weak walk from $a$ to $b$ in $T_n$. Thus deletion of any one vertex leaves all survivors weakly connected.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $a=b$, use the zero-step walk. Otherwise either $a<b$ or $b<a$, so a direct edge joins the two vertices in one orientation. Traversing that edge weakly gives a one-step walk whose endpoints both survive.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Infinite Robust Acyclic Family]
For every $n\geq3$, there is an acyclic network on $n$ vertices, containing three distinct vertices, that remains weakly connected after every single-vertex deletion.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $T_n$ and the distinct vertices $0,1,2$.
\end{proof}

The construction is intentionally dense. Its role is to refute a universal inference: if fragility followed merely from acyclicity, it would hold here. It does not. Alternate paths and underlying articulation structure, not acyclicity alone, govern deletion damage.

\section{Algorithms}
Canonical ranks can be computed by topological dynamic programming. Compute a topological order, initialize an empty ancestor bit set $B(v)$ at each vertex, and process vertices in that order. For every edge $u\to v$, perform
\[
 B(v)\leftarrow B(v)\cup B(u)\cup\{u\}.
\]
Then return $\rho(v)=|B(v)|$. Correctness follows by induction: each ancestor of $v$ reaches an immediate predecessor, and every inserted element reaches $v$. With ordinary sets the worst-case time is $O(NM)$ and storage $O(N^2)$ for $N$ vertices and $M$ edges. Packed bit sets reduce unions to approximately $O(MN/w)$ word operations, after an $O(N+M)$ topological sort, where $w$ is the machine word size.

To find a forced incomparable pair, store the first vertex encountered at every rank. A repeated rank returns a pair. Given the strict-rank invariant and $L<N$, correctness and success follow from the width--depth theorem. The cost is $O(N+L)$ time and $O(L)$ storage with an array.

To test deletion robustness directly, delete each vertex in turn and run breadth-first search in the underlying undirected graph on the survivors. This costs $O(N(N+M))$ time and $O(N+M)$ working space. Standard articulation-point algorithms can instead identify all vulnerable vertices in $O(N+M)$ time. For $T_n$, no search is needed because each surviving pair is directly adjacent in one orientation.

\section{Examples}
For the chain $0\to1\to2\to3$, the ancestor ranks are $0,1,2,3$. There is no rank collision. For the diamond
\[
0\to1,\quad0\to2,\quad1\to3,\quad2\to3,
\]
the ancestor sets are
\[
A(0)=\varnothing,\quad A(1)=A(2)=\{0\},\quad A(3)=\{0,1,2\}.
\]
The ranks are $0,1,1,3$, and vertices $1$ and $2$ are incomparable.

For $T_5$, vertex $j$ has ancestors $0,\ldots,j-1$, so the ranks are $0,1,2,3,4$. Deleting vertex $2$ leaves $0,1,3,4$, still pairwise adjacent in the underlying undirected graph. The same holds for any deletion. A chain and $T_5$ can therefore share the same rank sequence while having opposite interior-deletion behavior.

\section{Limits of structural inference}
A scale-free hypothesis such as
\[
 P(K=k)\sim Ck^{-\gamma}
\]
for theorem reuse is statistical, not a consequence of acyclicity. Chains, balanced trees, and strict total orders are all acyclic but have incompatible degree distributions. An empirical claim must specify whether $K$ counts direct reuse, transitive reuse, or another notion; it must also specify corpus version, treatment of definitions, tail cutoff, uncertainty, and comparison distributions.

Nor does acyclicity produce a universal list of hub theorems. Rankings can vary with domain, age, naming conventions, and abstraction boundaries. A result explicit in one corpus may be hidden inside a definition or interface in another. Historical prominence and graph centrality should therefore be measured separately.

Finally, high degree does not imply articulation. A high-degree vertex may have many alternate routes around it, while a modest-degree bridge may be essential. The robust total-order family makes this distinction exact.

\section{Applications and empirical protocol}
A disciplined study should begin with a versioned corpus and an explicit extraction policy. Direct references, transitive references, and references after collapsing definitional expansions should be compared. Cycles introduced by coarse aggregation should be identified and resolved or documented. Canonical ranks and rank-level widths can then be computed without presupposing a network-generation model.

Degree tails should be estimated by domain and rank as well as globally. A global heavy tail may be a mixture of heterogeneous layers. Deletion experiments should compare predictors including degree, articulation status, and counts of internally vertex-disjoint weak paths. Rank histograms expose antichain layers and suggest statements that can be studied or taught in parallel. Canonical rank can also constrain prerequisite search because every dependency ancestor must lie lower than its dependent.

\section{Future directions}
Five questions are immediate. First, are estimated tail exponents stable under direct, transitive, and definition-collapsed extraction? Second, how does antichain width grow with corpus size within individual domains? Third, do redundant path counts predict deletion damage better than degree? Fourth, do normalized hub rankings vary substantially across algebra, analysis, topology, and combinatorics? Fifth, does a heavy-tail exponent depend on canonical rank, with earlier layers exhibiting heavier reuse tails?

Theoretically, one may ask what robustness follows from combinations of acyclicity, minimum underlying degree, bounded width, and path redundancy. It is also useful to compare ancestor-count rank with longest-path depth under corpus extension. Ancestor rank measures accumulated support but can change globally when upstream material is added; longest-path depth captures chain complexity but discards breadth.

\section{Conclusion}
Finite acyclic dependency networks possess a canonical hierarchy: strict ancestor count rises along every dependency path. Any legal hierarchy with fewer levels than vertices forces incomparable statements, and one rank level has size at least $\lceil |V|/L\rceil$. Yet acyclicity does not imply fragility: strict total-order networks form an infinite family remaining weakly connected after every single-vertex deletion.

The boundary is therefore clear. Hierarchy and a width--depth tradeoff are universal order-theoretic consequences. Power laws, historical hubs, and deletion damage are corpus-dependent hypotheses requiring explicit measurement. Respecting that distinction turns the network metaphor into a rigorous, testable program.

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable

Vertex = int
Edge = tuple[Vertex, Vertex]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DependencyDAG:
    """A finite directed graph with vertices 0 through n-1."""

    n: int
    edges: tuple[Edge, ...]

    def adjacency(self) -> list[list[int]]:
        out = [[] for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u, v in self.edges:
            out[u].append(v)
        return out

    def topological_order(self) -> list[int]:
        out = self.adjacency()
        indegree = [0] * self.n
        for _, v in self.edges:
            indegree[v] += 1
        queue = deque(v for v in range(self.n) if indegree[v] == 0)
        order: list[int] = []
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            order.append(u)
            for v in out[u]:
                indegree[v] -= 1
                if indegree[v] == 0:
                    queue.append(v)
        if len(order) != self.n:
            raise ValueError("The graph contains a directed cycle")
        return order

    def ancestor_sets(self) -> list[set[int]]:
        """Compute all strict ancestors by topological dynamic programming."""
        out = self.adjacency()
        ancestors = [set() for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u in self.topological_order():
            for v in out[u]:
                ancestors[v].update(ancestors[u])
                ancestors[v].add(u)
        return ancestors

    def canonical_ranks(self) -> list[int]:
        return [len(items) for items in self.ancestor_sets()]

    def incomparable_pairs(self) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
        ancestors = self.ancestor_sets()
        return [
            (a, b)
            for a in range(self.n)
            for b in range(a + 1, self.n)
            if a not in ancestors[b] and b not in ancestors[a]
        ]

    def weakly_connected_after_deletion(self, deleted: int) -> bool:
        survivors = [v for v in range(self.n) if v != deleted]
        if len(survivors) <= 1:
            return True
        undirected = [set() for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u, v in self.edges:
            if u != deleted and v != deleted:
                undirected[u].add(v)
                undirected[v].add(u)
        seen = {survivors[0]}
        queue = deque([survivors[0]])
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            for v in undirected[u] - seen:
                seen.add(v)
                queue.append(v)
        return len(seen) == len(survivors)


def total_order_dag(n: int) -> DependencyDAG:
    """Return the robust acyclic graph with edge i -> j exactly when i < j."""
    return DependencyDAG(n, tuple((i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n)))


def graph_from_edges(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> DependencyDAG:
    return DependencyDAG(n, tuple(edges))


def print_graph_report(name: str, graph: DependencyDAG) -> None:
    ancestors = graph.ancestor_sets()
    ranks = graph.canonical_ranks()
    print(f"\n{name}")
    print("-" * len(name))
    print(f"vertices={graph.n}, edges={len(graph.edges)}")
    for v in range(graph.n):
        print(f"vertex {v}: ancestors={sorted(ancestors[v])}, rank={ranks[v]}")
    print(f"incomparable pairs: {graph.incomparable_pairs()}")
    robustness = [graph.weakly_connected_after_deletion(v) for v in range(graph.n)]
    print(f"weakly connected after deleting each vertex: {robustness}")


def demonstrate_width_depth() -> None:
    """Show that equal strict ranks produce an incomparable pair."""
    diamond = graph_from_edges(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])
    ranks = diamond.canonical_ranks()
    assert ranks == [0, 1, 1, 3]
    assert (1, 2) in diamond.incomparable_pairs()
    print_graph_report("Diamond: a rank collision forces width", diamond)


def demonstrate_robust_family(n: int = 7) -> None:
    """Check every deletion in a strict total-order DAG."""
    graph = total_order_dag(n)
    assert graph.canonical_ranks() == list(range(n))
    assert all(graph.weakly_connected_after_deletion(v) for v in range(n))
    print_graph_report(f"Strict total order on {n} vertices", graph)


def contrast_chain_and_total_order(n: int = 6) -> None:
    """Compare graphs with identical ranks but different deletion robustness."""
    chain = graph_from_edges(n, ((i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)))
    dense = total_order_dag(n)
    assert chain.canonical_ranks() == dense.canonical_ranks() == list(range(n))
    chain_status = [chain.weakly_connected_after_deletion(v) for v in range(n)]
    dense_status = [dense.weakly_connected_after_deletion(v) for v in range(n)]
    print("\nSame canonical ranks, different robustness")
    print("------------------------------------------")
    print(f"chain deletion status:       {chain_status}")
    print(f"total-order deletion status: {dense_status}")


def main() -> None:
    demonstrate_width_depth()
    demonstrate_robust_family()
    contrast_chain_and_total_order()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Numerical demonstrations for ranked finite dependency networks."""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable

Vertex = int
Edge = tuple[Vertex, Vertex]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DependencyDAG:
    """A finite directed graph with vertices 0 through n-1."""

    n: int
    edges: tuple[Edge, ...]

    def adjacency(self) -> list[list[int]]:
        out = [[] for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u, v in self.edges:
            out[u].append(v)
        return out

    def topological_order(self) -> list[int]:
        out = self.adjacency()
        indegree = [0] * self.n
        for _, v in self.edges:
            indegree[v] += 1
        queue = deque(v for v in range(self.n) if indegree[v] == 0)
        order: list[int] = []
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            order.append(u)
            for v in out[u]:
                indegree[v] -= 1
                if indegree[v] == 0:
                    queue.append(v)
        if len(order) != self.n:
            raise ValueError("The graph contains a directed cycle")
        return order

    def ancestor_sets(self) -> list[set[int]]:
        """Compute all strict ancestors by topological dynamic programming."""
        out = self.adjacency()
        ancestors = [set() for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u in self.topological_order():
            for v in out[u]:
                ancestors[v].update(ancestors[u])
                ancestors[v].add(u)
        return ancestors

    def canonical_ranks(self) -> list[int]:
        return [len(items) for items in self.ancestor_sets()]

    def incomparable_pairs(self) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
        ancestors = self.ancestor_sets()
        return [
            (a, b)
            for a in range(self.n)
            for b in range(a + 1, self.n)
            if a not in ancestors[b] and b not in ancestors[a]
        ]

    def weakly_connected_after_deletion(self, deleted: int) -> bool:
        survivors = [v for v in range(self.n) if v != deleted]
        if len(survivors) <= 1:
            return True
        undirected = [set() for _ in range(self.n)]
        for u, v in self.edges:
            if u != deleted and v != deleted:
                undirected[u].add(v)
                undirected[v].add(u)
        seen = {survivors[0]}
        queue = deque([survivors[0]])
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            for v in undirected[u] - seen:
                seen.add(v)
                queue.append(v)
        return len(seen) == len(survivors)

    """Return the robust acyclic graph with edge i -> j exactly when i < j."""
    return DependencyDAG(n, tuple((i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n)))


def graph_from_edges(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> DependencyDAG:
    return DependencyDAG(n, tuple(edges))

    ancestors = graph.ancestor_sets()
    ranks = graph.canonical_ranks()
    print(f"\n{name}")
    print("-" * len(name))
    print(f"vertices={graph.n}, edges={len(graph.edges)}")
    for v in range(graph.n):

    print(f"incomparable pairs: {graph.incomparable_pairs()}")

# Computational Evidence

## Small-case calculations

For the friendship graph with `n` triangles, the closed formula is

`P(F_n,q) = q ((q-1)(q-2))^n`.

| `n` | vertices | `P(F_n,2)` | `P(F_n,3)` | `P(F_n,6)` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| 1 | 3 | 0 | 6 | 120 |
| 2 | 5 | 0 | 12 | 2400 |
| 3 | 7 | 0 | 24 | 48000 |
| 4 | 9 | 0 | 48 | 960000 |

For every `n ≥ 1`, the first positive palette size is three. Under the imposed three-category emotional floor, the same conclusion also holds for `n = 0`.

A one-edge graph supplies the smallest counterexample to the proposed universal bipartite root at two: it has two proper two-colorings, obtained by exchanging the two colors between its endpoints.

## Sequence search

At the minimum admissible palette the friendship counts begin `3, 6, 12, 24, 48`, a geometric sequence. At six colors they begin `6, 120, 2400, 48000, 960000`, also geometric. No OEIS identifier is needed for these elementary geometric sequences.

## Counterexample hunt

The universal statement “every bipartite graph has chromatic value zero at two” fails immediately for a single edge. The corrected behavior is the opposite for any two-colorable graph: existence of a proper two-coloring makes the value at two positive. The emotional floor must therefore be imposed as a modeling constraint rather than deduced as a polynomial root.

## Structural comparison

The ratio `P(F_n,6) / P(F_n,3)` equals `2 · 10^n`. Each additional triangle doubles the number of assignments at the minimum palette but multiplies the six-palette count by twenty. This motivates comparing the ratio under other patterns of gluing triangles.

    ∃ η' : ℝ → ℂ, IsSmoothLoop (fun θ => (γ θ) ^ k) η' := by
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ : ∃ n : ℕ, k = n ∨ k = -n := by
    exact ⟨ Int.natAbs k, by cases abs_cases k <;> simp +decide [ * ] ⟩;
  rcases hn with ( rfl | rfl );
  · exact ⟨ _, smoothLoop_pow_and_winding hγ n |>.1 ⟩;
  · have := smoothLoop_pow_and_winding ( smoothLoop_inv hγ ) n; aesop;

/-

modes, independently powering the modes and multiplying them gives the integral
linear combination of their charges.
-/
theorem winding_mul_zpow {γ γ' δ δ' : ℝ → ℂ}
    (hγ : IsSmoothLoop γ γ') (hδ : IsSmoothLoop δ δ') (k l : ℤ) :
    winding (fun θ => (γ θ) ^ k * (δ θ) ^ l) =
      (k : ℂ) * winding γ + (l : ℂ) * winding δ := by
  -- We will obtain the derivative witnesses for the power loops via smoothLoop_zpow.
  obtain ⟨ηγ, hηγ⟩ := smoothLoop_zpow hγ k
  obtain ⟨ηδ, hηδ⟩ := smoothLoop_zpow hδ l;
  rw [ winding_mul hηγ hηδ, winding_zpow hγ k, winding_zpow hδ l ]
